extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and professionals (physicians, naturalists, philosophers/critics) reading Popular Science Monthly
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative principles for composing and judging critical responses to scholarly or popular works, together with separate practical guidance for medical treatment of liver disorder and evaluation of plant oils as discussed in the magazine pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disproving statements which have not been made
rubrics_metrics.description: "Criticism would be greatly diminished in bulk if there were excluded from it all that part devoted to disproving statements which have not been made."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: constructing and refuting positions the original author never held (straw-man). Example: Guthrie's work is criticized as largely a misstatement of Spencer's views followed by refutation of the misstatements. Good criticism should target the author's actual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately represent the author's actual views
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not misstate fundamental views of an author and then proceed to refute the misstatements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from Spencer: extract brief passages showing what the author's views actually are before critiquing; avoid treating the author's symbols or descriptions as literal claims about external reality when the author treats them as symbols. Anti-patterns include treating symbolic/formal language as the author's ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote and attribute phrases correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tacitly make an author responsible for phrases or expressions that are not theirs (misattribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer gives the example where Professor Birks quotes Mr. Mill's expression as though it were Spencer's. Critical practice: ensure quoted phrases are properly attributed; avoid creating false associations that make incoherences appear to belong to the target author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by the author's latest expression; allow corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usual in literary criticism to judge an author by the latest expression of his views and allow any corrections he has made to stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an author revises or suppresses passages to correct or avoid side issues, critics should treat the corrected/latest statements as authoritative rather than pouncing on earlier versions without acknowledging changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective fragment-quoting that misleads (quote in context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not quote isolated words or short fragments out of context to imply a view the author did not hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Birks quotes 'appearance without reality is unthinkable' then comments in a way that misleads the reader. Good criticism quotes enough context to preserve sense and meaning; anti-patterns involve cropping sentences to change sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force the author into false binary alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid setting up narrow alternative positions and assuming the author must accept one or the other as described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: critics who present two exclusive positions about matter and motion and then assume the author endorses one of them when the author's view is different or more nuanced. Critic should allow for intermediary or alternative conceptualizations the author may use (e.g., symbols vs. ontological claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish laws from assertions of existence; be precise about what is a law versus what is claimed to exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate asserting a law deducible a priori with asserting the existence of the entity to which the law would apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer's example: asserting that central forces vary inversely as the square of the distance (a law) is not the same as asserting that gravitation necessarily exists as a fact; critics should not transform a statement about law into a claim about existence and then criticize that supposed claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with technical and philosophical terminology (avoid equivocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware misleading connotations of words such as 'appearance' or 'phenomenon' and avoid conflating popular meanings with metaphysical or technical senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer argues that critics who construe 'phenomenon' only as 'visible thing' misunderstand philosophical usage. Guidance: clarify definitions and intended senses before criticizing; use neutral or clarified terms (e.g., 'effect') if necessary to avoid equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on essential arguments; avoid evasion by raising side issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppressing or avoiding non-essential side-issues (or not allowing critics to open them) can be legitimate to keep attention on the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer notes he omitted a passage to prevent opponents from evading the chapter's general argument via a side issue. Critics should avoid diverting critique into tangential matters that do not bear on the central thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume the author accepts scientific doctrines without textual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not tacitly assume the author endorses particular scientific doctrines (e.g., the doctrine of potential energy) unless the author explicitly does so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer points out Birks assumed he accepted the doctrine of potential energy and then argued consequences. Good critics verify whether the author accepts disputed scientific positions before using them as premises for refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain critical fairness and avoid deliberate misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate misrepresentation to score rhetorical points (e.g., 'doing God service' by misrepresenting an opponent) is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spencer criticizes Birks for tacitly making Spencer responsible for others' incongruities. Guidance: critics should act honestly, attribute positions fairly, and avoid rhetorical devices that distort the opponent's views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical remedy: use of dilute nitro-hydrochloric (nitro-muriatic) acid for liver disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten minims of dilute nitro-hydrochloric acid, either before or immediately after meals, combined with some aromatic and carminative (such as chloroform and cardamoms or orange), and from five to ten minims of tincture of nux vomica where the nervous depression is great, is a most efficient remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration details: 10 minims before/immediately after meals; combine with aromatic carminatives; add 5–10 minims tincture nux vomica when nervous depression is marked. Note: original text states 'we do not know how it acts' — guidance is empirical/historical rather than mechanistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise regimen for stimulating the liver
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise is necessary to keep the liver in order; a brisk trot on horseback for fifteen minutes will cause more pressure upon and stimulation of the liver than a lazy lounge of an hour or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: should not be taken immediately after a meal; for busy men the best time is before breakfast. Pre-exercise snack: a cup of milk or small cup of tea/coffee and a piece of bread and butter or a biscuit may be taken just before starting. Walking for short, gentle periods may be insufficient to stimulate liver.

rubrics_metrics.name: General regimen to reduce nervous exhaustion in brain-workers
rubrics_metrics.description: By careful attention to the removal of waste products, prevention of absorption of poisonous substances from the intestine, regulation of the diet, regulation of the bowels, and exercise, nervous exhaustion and depression in brain-workers may be greatly diminished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multimodal approach: focus on digestive health (avoid absorption of poisons), ensure regular bowel function, regulate diet, and include appropriate exercise. These are preventive/mitigative measures rather than guaranteed cures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for evaluating oil-plants and their oils
rubrics_metrics.description: Important factors: abundance and quality of oil yield (e.g., Carapa Guianensis notable for both), percentage yield from nuts/kernels, physical properties of the oil (clarity when cold-pressed, amber color, tendency to give a solid crystalline deposit on standing), utility for soap-making (degree of hardness), lubricating and illumination qualities, and susceptibility to spoilage of fruits and paste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraction and yield notes: natives boil kernels, make a paste and sun-heat it or press in bags; nuts with coverings yield ≈36% oil, cleaned kernels ≈60%; Omphalea yields ≈64.58%. Economic guidance: make oil where nuts grow because fruits do not keep well (mold, grubs, spoilage); cold-pressed oil is clear and amber; refined oil used for lubrication and gives good light. Soap-making guidance: oils that give too soft soaps can be mixed with carapa oil for hardness.
